props.title: Gates of Heaven

sections.content: Gates of Heaven revolutionized documentary filmmaking through Errol Morris's unflinching yet deeply empathetic look at pet cemeteries in California. The film's deceptively simple premise - interviewing pet owners and cemetery operators - unveils profound meditations on death, love, and human nature. Morris's technique of letting subjects speak directly to camera (later dubbed the "Interrotron" method) influenced countless documentarians like The Thin Blue Line (1988) and became a cornerstone of modern documentary style. Werner Herzog famously ate his shoe after losing a bet that Morris wouldn't complete the film - documented in Les Blank's Werner Herzog Eats His Shoe (1980).

sections.content: The influence of Gates of Heaven extends beyond just technique - it helped establish the "American eccentric" documentary subgenre. Films like American Movie (1999) and Crumb (1994) followed Morris's lead in finding profound truth and humanity in seemingly bizarre or marginal subjects. The film's ability to extract universal themes from specific situations became a template for personal documentaries like Sherman's March (1986) and Grey Gardens (1975).

Morris's innovative approach to interview subjects - letting them talk at length without interruption while maintaining direct eye contact through the Interrotron - created an intimacy that influenced directors like Agnès Varda in The Gleaners and I (2000) and Joshua Oppenheimer in The Act of Killing (2012). This technique allows subjects to reveal themselves in ways traditional documentary interviews rarely achieve. SUBHEAD: Impact on Contemporary Documentary

sections.content: The film's legacy is particularly visible in modern hybrid documentaries that blur the line between fiction and non-fiction. Works like Stories We Tell (2012) and The Act of Killing (2012) share Morris's interest in how people construct narratives about their lives. His influence can be seen in the patient, observational style of contemporary documentarians like Frederick Wiseman (Ex Libris (2017)) and the personal essay films of Ross McElwee.
